AnovaLab: AnovaLab help 1/9: What one-way ANOVA asks
H₀: every group has the same population mean μ.
ANOVA splits the total spread (SS) in two:
between: n × (group mean - grand mean)²
within: (value - its own group mean)²
MS = SS / df;  F = MS between / MS within.
If H₀ is true, F is near 1 and follows the
F(k - 1, N - k) curve; p = P(F this big | H₀).
A small p is evidence that SOME mean differs:
not which (Pairs page), not how much (eta²).
eta² = SS between / SS total; omega² (Hays)
subtracts the part chance alone would give.
Every value counts: 0 and negatives are data.

AnovaLab help 2/9: Welch and the checks
The F test assumes equal spreads (and roughly normal groups).
Welch's F (1951) drops equal spreads: each group is weighted
by n / s².
Levene's test (Brown-Forsythe form) runs the one-way F on
|value - group median|; non-normal data affect it little.
Bartlett's χ² compares the s² directly: it is misled by
non-normal data.
In the insect-spray preset, s runs from 1.7 to 6.2 and Levene's
test flags it; compare the ordinary F with Welch's.
A check that is not significant is not proof of equal spreads: with
small groups the checks often miss real differences.
Dots page: look at the spreads yourself.

AnovaLab help 3/9: Which pairs differ?
Many t-tests raise the chance of at least one false alarm; these
keep that chance at α for the whole set (the family):
Tukey-Kramer: q = |diff|/√(MSW/2 (1/n₁+1/n₂)) on the
studentized range (it asks before it runs, since it is slow).
Bonferroni: raw t p × m pairs (simple, safe).
Holm: Bonferroni done in steps; never less power than
Bonferroni.

AnovaLab help 6/9: Randomized blocks
Each block (a judge, a person) gets every
treatment once: repeated measures.
Blocks differ a lot, and that spread is taken
OUT of the error: SSE = SST - SSTr - SSBlocks.
F (treatments) = MS treatments / MS error.
partial eta² = SSTr / (SSTr + SSE).
The Table page also shows the one-way F that
ignores the blocks: judges' ratings give
p = 0.048 that way, far smaller with blocks.
Assumes no block × treatment interaction
(and, for repeated measures, sphericity).
Plot: one gray line per block.

AnovaLab help 7/9: One and two variances
One σ: χ² = (n - 1) s² / σ₀², df n - 1.
CI for σ²: ((n-1)s²/χ² upper, (n-1)s²/χ² lower)
Two σ: F = s₁² / s₂², df n₁ - 1 and n₂ - 1.
CI for σ₁²/σ₂²: (F/F upper, F/F lower).
Two-sided p = 2 × the smaller tail.  The curve
shades that tail and the other tail of EQUAL
area (blue), and both critical regions (red).
These tests trust normal data much more than
tests of means do; skewed data mislead them.
For several groups, Levene (Checks) is safer.

CICatcher: CICatcher help 1/6: 95 % of WHAT?
Each line is the interval from ONE sample.
The green line is the truth (μ or p): the method never sees it. A
blue line caught it (the interval contains it); a red line missed it.
The 95 % is the share of intervals the METHOD catches in the
long run, not a property of any one interval. Keep adding
samples: the 'all' rate at the top of the screen settles near the
confidence level.
Any one interval either caught μ or missed it.
So say 'we are 95 % confident' -- meaning the method catches
the truth 95 % of the time -- not 'a 95 % chance μ is in
THIS interval'.

CICatcher help 2/6: Level and width; z and t
Drag the right edge (or ⇅): a higher level uses a bigger critical
value, so EVERY line grows, red lines turn blue and the catch rate
rises. 99 % catches more, but its longer lines give a less
precise answer.
z:  ± z × σ/√(n) uses the TRUE σ, so every z line has the
same length.
t:  ± t × s/√(n) uses the sample's s.
s changes from sample to sample, so t lines differ in length, so
t's critical value is bigger than z's to make up for that:
z with s at n = 10 would catch only 91.8 %.
t critical value: not needed yet (no t run)

CICatcher help 3/6: Wald and Wilson
Wald:  ± z × √((1 - )/n), the textbook interval. Center and
width both come from , which fails when n × p is small:
at p = 0.10, n = 20 Wald catches only 87.6 % (exact binomial; it
claims 95 %).
12.2 % of those samples have  = 0: the Wald interval has ZERO
width and must miss.
Wilson (score) takes its SE from each possible p, not from ,
and keeps every p within z SEs of : never zero width, center
pulled toward 1/2. Same p and n: 95.7 %.
Wald needs n × p and n × (1 - p) to be 10 or more; at p = 0.10,
n = 100 it reaches 93.2 %.
Gray on the axis: impossible values (below 0, above 1). Only
Wald lines can reach them.
any key or tap = next page, Esc = done
CICatcher help 4/6: Exact intervals
Exact (Clopper-Pearson) uses no normal curve:
it keeps every p for which your count is not in either α/2 tail of
Binomial(n, p).
A count has only n + 1 possible values, so no interval can catch
exactly 95 % at every p.
Exact makes sure it is NEVER LESS: at n = 20 its worst case over
every p is 95.8 %.
At p = 0.10, n = 20 it catches 98.9 % (Wilson 95.7 %, Wald 87.6
%); at 80 % or 90 % it still catches 95.7 %. The cost: longer lines
(wider intervals).
0 yeses: from 0 to 1 - (α/2)^(1/n), 0.168 at n = 20 and 95 %.
Tap such a line: the panel shows that end as the CAS writes it.
exact ends: bisection on BINOMIAL_CDF, checked

CICatcher help 5/6: A criminal-justice example
A city asks n = 100 residents: 'Are you afraid
to walk alone at night?' 38 say yes, so
 = 0.38 and the 95 % Wald interval is
RIGHT: 'We are 95 % confident the true share
is between 28.5 % and 47.5 %': the method
catches the truth 95 % of the time.
WRONG: 'There is a 95 % chance the true share
is in this interval.' The share is fixed;
this interval caught it or it did not.
Try it: Wilson, p = 0.38, n = 100, then +50.

FitCheck help 2/8: Goodness of fit
χ² GOODNESS OF FIT.  E = N × (the cell's
proportion under H₀): what the cell would hold
if H₀ were exactly right.  χ² = sum of (O -
E)²/E: big when the counts are far from E.  df
= k - 1 - m, where m counts the parameters
estimated from the same data (Poisson λ: 1;
binomial p: 1; normal μ and σ: 2).  p = the
right tail of the χ² curve (Curve page).
Each cell's contribution (O - E)²/E is the
magenta strip under the bars; (O - E)/√E is
its signed square root: beyond ±2 the cell
stands out.

FitCheck help 3/8: Small counts and Merge
The χ² curve gives a trustworthy p only when
the E are not too small: every E ≥ 5, or
Cochran's rule (at most 20% of the E below 5
and none below 1).  FitCheck checks EVERY
cell.  If the rule fails, Merge joins
neighboring cells, the smallest E first, and
the Test page names exactly which cells were
merged (Unmrg undoes it).

FitCheck help 4/8: Benford, Poisson, binomial
BENFORD'S LAW.  In many collections of amounts
spread over several powers of ten the leading
digit d turns up with probability log₁₀(1 +
1/d): a 1 about 30.1% of the time, a 9 only
4.6%.  The first two digits: log₁₀(1 + 1/(10a
+ b)).  In the two-digit test numbers below 10
are left out (they have no second digit).
Nigrini's MAD is the average gap between the
actual and Benford's proportions.  The orange
curve on the bars is Benford's law.
POISSON: λ is estimated as the mean count; the
last cell is the tail (K or more), so the E
add up to N; df = k - 2.  BINOMIAL: p
estimated (df = k - 2) or typed (df = k - 1).

FitCheck help 6/8: Reading p; the exact test
A small p is evidence against normality; a
large p is NOT proof of it.  With a big n,
tiny departures give tiny p: the Q-Q plot
shows how big the departure is.
EXACT BINOMIAL TEST.  X ~ Binomial(n, p₀).
The two-sided p adds P(X = k) over every k no
more likely than the observed x (R's
binom.test, SciPy's binomtest).  Everything is
done in logs, so a p of 10^-145 (the Castaneda
jury preset) is still printed as a number.
The plot shows how many SDs x is from E, the
reasoning the Supreme Court used in Castaneda
v. Partida (1977).

RankLab: RankLab help 1/7: What it does
Rank tests replace each value by its rank, so an outlier counts no
more than the next value, and no normal population is assumed.
Tied values share the average of the ranks they span: the
MIDRANK.  Every test here uses midranks and the
tie-corrected variance.
Each test opens on its Result page.  ⇅ turn the pages: Result, a
picture, the null distribution (and Dunn pairs for Kruskal-
Wallis).  Soft keys: Result, Plot, Null, the 4th key (Exact/Normal,
or what that page switches), Tails, More (Help, Dunn or
Data, Menu).

RankLab help 3/7: Sign test, signed-rank
Both test H₀: the median of d is 0.  Zeros
are dropped: n counts the nonzero d only.
SIGN: S+ = number of d > 0, Binomial(n, 1/2)
under H₀; exact p from BINOMIAL_CDF; two-
sided = 2 × the smaller tail (at most 1).
SIGNED-RANK: rank |d| (midranks); T+ = the
sum of the ranks of d > 0.  Under H₀ each
sign is + or - with chance 1/2, 2^n patterns;
RankLab counts them all (ties too), n ≤ 50.
Effect r = (T+ - T-)/(n(n+1)/2).  Estimate:
Hodges-Lehmann = the median of all Walsh
averages (d_i + d_j)/2, i ≤ j (n ≤ 100).

RankLab help 4/7: Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis
MANN-WHITNEY: rank both groups together;
U₁ = R₁ - n₁(n₁ + 1)/2 = the (X, Y) pairs with
X > Y (ties count 1/2).  Exact: every split
of the N ranks is equally likely; RankLab
counts them (no ties, n₁ n₂ ≤ 400).  Ties:
normal, tie-corrected, continuity corrected.
P(X > Y) + ties/2 = U₁/(n₁ n₂); rank-biserial
r = (U₁ - U₂)/(n₁ n₂).  Hodges-Lehmann shift.
KRUSKAL-WALLIS: H compares the k mean ranks;
p from χ²(k - 1); epsilon² = H/(N - 1).
DUNN: z for each pair of mean ranks, Holm-
adjusted over the k(k - 1)/2 pairs.

FRIEDMAN: rank within each block (row); Q compares the
treatments' rank sums, p from χ²(k - 1).  Kendall's
W = Q/(b(k - 1)): 0 = the blocks disagree, 1 = every block ranks
the treatments the same.

KENDALL tau-b = (concordant - discordant)
pairs / √((n₀ - n₁)(n₀ - n₂)); exact p without ties (n ≤ 30), else z
(tie-corrected).

RiskLab: RiskLab help 1/8: Logistic regression
A risk tool turns facts about a person into a
score that predicts an outcome Y (1 = re-
arrested, 0 = not).  Logistic regression:
ln(P/(1 - P)) = b₀ + b₁x₁ + ... + bk xk
odds = P/(1 - P); OR = e^b multiplies the odds
for +1 in x, the other x held fixed.
Fit: Newton-Raphson (IRLS), b → b + I^-1 U,
U = X'(y - μ), I = X'WX, W = μ(1 - μ),
until each step < 1E-9 (Hosmer & Lemeshow
2000; Agresti 2013).  SE = √(diag. of I^-1).
Wald z = b/SE.  LR χ² = 2(lnL - lnL₀), df k.
McFadden R² = 1 - lnL/lnL₀ (McFadden 1974):
not a share of variance explained.
Page 1/8, any key = next, Esc = leave
RiskLab help 2/8: Separation, collinearity
If some x (or a mix of x) puts every Y = 1 above every Y = 0, the
likelihood keeps rising as |b| grows: no finite estimate
(Albert & Anderson 1984).  RiskLab warns when the fit has not
converged in 25 steps, the fitted line orders Y perfectly, or I
turns singular.  Remedies: drop or merge that x, or a penalised
(Firth) fit, not offered here.
Collinear x (one a mix of the others) make I singular too: no SEs.
Speed: each step of the fit goes through every row; Rossi's 432
rows need about 7 passes.  On a G1 that is slow (a progress bar
shows it; Esc stops it).

RiskLab help 3/8: The ROC curve and the AUC
Flag 'high risk' if the score ≥ a cut-off.
TPR (sensitivity) = flagged share of Y = 1;
FPR = 1 - specificity = flagged share of Y=0.
Moving the cut-off from high to low traces the
ROC curve from (0, 0) to (1, 1); tied scores
make a diagonal step.  AUC = area under it =
P(a random Y = 1 scores above a random Y = 0),
ties 1/2: the Mann-Whitney U/(n₁ n₀).
0.5 = chance, 1 = perfect.  SE: DeLong et al.
(1988); CI = AUC ± 1.96 SE, cut at 0 and 1.
Tap the AUC line: Hanley-McNeil's SE (1982),
which assumes a shape; DeLong's does not.
A model's AUC on its own data is optimistic.
Page 3/8, any key = next, Esc = leave
RiskLab help 4/8: Cut-offs and trade-offs
A lower cut-off flags more people: more TP (sensitivity up) and
more FP (specificity down).  No cut-off avoids both errors.
PPV = TP/(TP + FP): of those flagged, the share with Y = 1.  It
depends on the base rate: the same sensitivity and specificity
give a lower PPV where Y = 1 is rarer.
NPV = TN/(TN + FN).
Choosing a cut-off is choosing which error matters more: the
statistics show the trade-off, but they cannot say which error
is worse.
COMPAS deciles: 1-4 low, 5-7 medium, 8-10 high; ProPublica
took 5 and up as high risk.
Page 4/8, any key = next, Esc = leave
RiskLab help 5/8: Calibration, H-L test
Calibrated: of people given P = 0.3, about 30% have Y = 1.
RiskLab sorts by predicted P into 10 groups (ties kept together),
or one group per score level, and compares observed O with
expected E = sum of P in each group:
HL = sum of (O - E)²/(E(1 - E/n)), df = groups - 2
(Hosmer & Lemeshow 1980).  Weaknesses: it depends on the
number of groups and on how ties are cut (software differs); it
has low power with small n, and with large n a tiny misfit is
'significant' (Hosmer et al. 1997).
A large p is no proof of good calibration.
Gray bars: pred ± 1.96 SE, a rough guide.
For a score such as COMPAS's, pred is the P from RiskLab's own
logistic fit of Y on the score.
Page 5/8, any key = next, Esc = leave
RiskLab help 6/8: Fairness definitions
Predictive parity: the same score means the same risk in both
groups, so PPV is equal (Northpointe: Dieterich et al. 2016, with
equal AUC, 'accuracy equity').
Error-rate balance: equal FPR and equal FNR in both groups
(ProPublica: Angwin et al.
2016).  When base rates differ and prediction is not perfect,
these cannot all hold at once:
Chouldechova (2017) for PPV, FPR and FNR;
Kleinberg, Mullainathan & Raghavan (2016) for calibration vs
equal average scores among Y=1 and among Y=0.  Both sides'
numbers can be right at once, because they answer different
questions.
